newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai economy set for sluggish 1997 growth - KTT.
newsitem.headline: Thai economy set for sluggish 1997 growth - KTT.

text.p: The Thai economy is set to grow by between 6.25 and 6.50 percent in 1997 as high domestic interest rates restrain an early economic recovery, broker Krungthai Thanakit Plc (KTT) said in a report on Wednesday.

"The Bank of Thailand forecasts, published in late December, include GDP growth for the year (1997) of 7.1 percent, representing something of a recovery from a 1996 number likely to emerge at around 6.7 percent. We regard this as being somewhat too optimistic," it said in a new report.
Thailand's economy was afflicted by a series of problems last year and the central bank has forecast 6.7 percent growth in 1996, it lowest level for a decade.

"Both consumer and business confidence were clearly hit very hard by the downturn in 1996. We believe that it is unlikely that there will be an early change of attitudes on a scale which would permit economic growth to accelerate this year," it said.
Pressure on the baht, which came under speculative attack in 1996, should ease in coming months, KTT added.

Although the easing of such pressures should see interest rates fall by some two percentage points in 1997, the size of the expected cuts would be insufficient to spur an early economic recovery, the firm said.

"We believe that the need to keep rates high (although not as high as they are now) will be among the factors tending to prevent the real economy from making an early or strong recovery," the report said.
Another year of slower growth will keep inflation at bay and depress demand for imports which should help improve the wide trade and current account deficits, the firm said.

"We expect the 1997 import growth figure will be thoroughly depressed by lack of demand. Whereas the the Bank of Thailand is forecasting eight percent, we believe the outcome is more likely to be in the region of five percent," the firm said.
Krungthai Thanakit said the resulting reduction should see Thailand's troubled current account deficit fall to 7.3 percent of GDP in 1997, against a forecast 8.4 percent of GDP in 1996.
The firm projected export growth in 1997 at 7.7 percent.
Official statistics showing export growth contracted during 1996 were distorted by massive tax frauds in 1995 during which Thailand exports officially grew by 24 percent, the firm said.
Export growth in 1995 and 1996 was more likely to have averaged 10 percent each year, the report said.
